questions.question: Three copies of the same model vote on an answer. When does the vote fail to help?
options: When the copies tend to make the same mistake, so wrong answers form a majority
questions.explanation: Voting relies on mistakes scattering; correlated errors defeat it.

questions.question: Why does the simulation use common random numbers?
options: So every strategy starts from identical first answers, and differences come from the strategy rather than luck
questions.explanation: A paired comparison removes noise between strategies.

questions.question: Debate matched voting's accuracy here at three times the calls. Why didn't it do better?
options: Agents could only adopt each other's answers; nobody brought new evidence or a better argument
questions.explanation: Without new information, debate converges where a vote would.

questions.question: A critic catches 50% of errors but objects to 40% of right answers. What happens?
options: It breaks about as many right answers as it fixes wrong ones
It always helps on hard questions
questions.explanation: Every false alarm risks a right answer being redone wrong.

questions.question: What gave the biggest gain with the fewest model calls?
options: A checker with a tool that recomputes the answer
questions.explanation: Evidence beats opinions, and it only triggers redos when the answer is actually wrong.

questions.question: You must use model-based voting on a task with no tool check. How can you reduce correlated errors?
options: Use more copies of the same prompt
Use different models, prompts or tools for each voter
questions.explanation: Diversity is what makes votes independent.
